articles.title: Trump floats rebranding artificial intelligence as super intelligence
articles.summary: "The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said told the UN. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing."
articles.body:
Donald Trump has a penchant for branding and in his speech he gave artificial intelligence a new name: super intelligence.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful," he added. "Welcome to the new world of super intelligence - SI," he went on to say.

Trump has previously argued that whoever wins AI, wins, and he is firmly against regulation. But that puts him at odds with many here.

The question is whether the slow pace of diplomacy can keep up with AI’s rapid development.

articles.title: David Almeida propõe ampliar emprego e renda no Amazonas | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do Avante ao governo do Amazonas participou de debate nesta terça-feira (22), onde falou sobre geração de emprego e renda e citou ações realizadas durante a gestão dele como prefeito de Manaus.
articles.summary: Em debate para as Eleições 2026, o candidato David Almeida detalhou como pretende usar obras em escolas e UBSs para movimentar a economia do Amazonas.
articles.body:
David Almeida promete ampliar geração de emprego e renda no Amazonas. — Foto: Reprodução/Rede Amazônica

O candidato ao governo do Amazonas, David Almeida (Avante), participou de um debate em uma emissora de TV local, na manhã desta terça-feira (22). Durante o encontro, ele falou sobre propostas para ampliar a geração de emprego e renda no estado e citou investimentos públicos como uma das formas de movimentar a economia.

David Almeida disputa o governo pela coligação “Pra Cima, Amazonas”, formada por Avante, Solidariedade, PRD, PDT, DC e Agir. O candidato é ex-prefeito de Manaus, cumpriu três mandatos como deputado estadual e assumiu interinamente o Governo do Amazonas em 2017.

Entre as propostas apresentadas por David está o uso de investimentos e obras públicas para ampliar as oportunidades de trabalho no Amazonas. Ele citou a construção de escolas, Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBSs) e obras de pavimentação como ações que, segundo ele, podem gerar empregos e renda.

“O emprego e a renda vêm quando você tem investimento. Quando você faz uma escola, quando você faz uma UBS, quando você faz pavimentação, você gera emprego, gera renda e movimenta a economia”, afirmou.

A agenda do candidato começou pela manhã, com participação no debate da emissora de TV, às 9h45. Às 17h, David Almeida participou de uma caminhada no bairro Manoa, na Zona Norte de Manaus. À noite, às 20h, está prevista uma reunião com lideranças no Tarumã-Açu.

articles.summary: Saiba as principais atividades dos concorrentes do pleito deste ano.
articles.body:
Candidatos ao governo do Acre nas eleições de 2026 — Foto: Reprodução

O g1 informa todos os dias as atividades de campanha dos candidatos ao governo do Acre nas eleições deste ano. Confira abaixo como foi nesta terça-feira (22).

Thor Dantas (PSB), Dr. Luisinho (Agir) e Eudo Raffael (PCB) não divulgaram as agendas.

Alan Rick (Republicanos) cumpriu agendas no Alto Acre durante a manhã e a tarde. Na região, participou de caminhada, carreata, comício e visitou frigoríficos. À noite, se reúne com apoiadores de candidato a deputado estadual na capital.

Mailza Assis (PP) gravou programa eleitoral, participou de encontro com a educação e se reuniu com lideranças.

Tião Bocalom (PSDB) se reuniu com trabalhadores de uma empresa privada na capital. Ele ouviu demandas e apresentou propostas do plano de governo. Durante a visita, falou sobre a importância da geração de empregos.

“Continuar o trabalho de rua, conversando com as pessoas, o que eu sempre fiz na minha vida, todas as minhas eleições. Nunca tive uma eleição fácil, quando eu venho pra uma reunião como essa daqui, numa empresa que é nossa, que produz uma quantidade grande, que gera muito emprego”, declarou.

articles.title: Ronaldo Caiado: Soberania está entregue ao crime organizado | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-governador e candidato à presidência pelo PSD deu declaração antes de carreata realizada em Morrinhos (GO). Caiado disse ainda que pretende qualificar as organizações criminosas como 'terroristas'.
articles.summary: O candidato Ronaldo Caiado defende o combate ao crime organizado e a retomada de territórios para garantir a soberania brasileira em agenda em Goiás.
articles.body:
Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) antes de carreata em Morrinhos, Goiás — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

O candidato à Presidência da República Ronaldo Caiado ( PSD ) falou sobre resgatar territórios no combate ao crime organizado como parte de sua proposta de governo. A declaração foi dada à imprensa antes de uma carreata realizada em Morrinhos , no sul de Goiás, nesta terça-feira (22).

"Todos nós sabemos que a soberania brasileira hoje está entregue, [em] grande parte do território brasileiro, às facções criminosas, onde o Estado não entra", afirmou o candidato e ex-governador de Goiás.

Caiado disse ainda que pretende qualificar as organizações criminosas como "terroristas" e desenvolver convênios com estados limítrofes (aqueles que fazem divisa com outras nações) na proteção das divisas brasileiras.

O candidato do PSD também declarou que não aceitará o que chamou de "ingerência de qualquer outro país em relação ao nosso território".

Caiado quer criar provas de proficiência em todas as faculdades: 'Nós vamos respeitar o dinheiro do cidadão'

Nesta terça-feira (22), o candidato também realizaria carreata no município de Buriti Alegre, no sul de Goiás, e uma reunião política em Luziânia, no Entorno do DF. No entanto, as agendas foram canceladas devido ao mau tempo, segundo a assessoria.

articles.title: Orleans Brandão cumpre agenda em Vila Nova dos Martírios e apresenta propostas para a juventude | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do MDB participou de reunião com apoiadores e carreata no município; propostas incluem ampliação do Trabalho Jovem, qualificação profissional e escolas em tempo integral.
articles.summary: Candidato do MDB participou de reunião com apoiadores e carreata no município; propostas incluem ampliação do Trabalho Jovem, qualificação profissional e escolas em tempo integral.
articles.body:
O candidato ao governo do Maranhão Orleans Brandão, do Movimento Democrático Brasileiro (MDB), cumpriu agenda nesta terça-feira (22), em Vila Nova dos Martírios, na região Tocantina do Maranhão.

Durante a visita ao município, Orleans participou de uma reunião com apoiadores e eleitores e de uma carreata pelas ruas da cidade.

O candidato apresentou propostas voltadas para a juventude, como a ampliação do programa Trabalho Jovem, investimentos em qualificação profissional e a expansão das escolas em tempo integral.

Orleans afirmou que pretende ampliar o número de vagas do programa Trabalho Jovem e investir na formação profissional dos estudantes.“E eu tenho falado em dobrar esse programa. Então, vou entrar com foco muito grande no trabalho jovem. Também vou levar a qualificação profissional através das escolas de tempo integral”, declarou.

O candidato também disse que pretende investir no esporte de base e criar uma complementação ao programa Pé-de-Meia, do governo federal, para estudantes do Maranhão.

Orleans Brandão (MDB) — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Mirante

As eleições de 2026 serão realizadas em 4 de outubro, no primeiro turno. Caso seja necessário, o segundo turno ocorrerá em 25 de outubro para os cargos de presidente da República e governador.

Na votação, os eleitores escolherão candidatos aos cargos de deputado estadual, deputado federal, dois senadores, governador e presidente.

A campanha eleitoral segue até 3 de outubro, véspera do primeiro turno. Em caso de segundo turno, a propaganda será retomada e poderá ocorrer até 24 de outubro.

articles.title: Falha em GPS usado por aviões da Embraer afeta voos da Azul | G1
articles.standfirst: Azul disse que instabilidade global no sistema está afetando operações de seus aviões da linha E2.
articles.summary: Azul disse que instabilidade global no sistema está afetando operações de seus aviões da linha E2.
articles.body:
Avião E195-E2, da Azul, em foto de 2019 — Foto: Luíza Veneziani/G1

A companhia aérea Azul afirmou nesta terça-feira (22) que uma instabilidade global no sistema de GPS está afetando a operação de seus aviões da linha E2, fabricados pela Embraer.

Em comunicado, a Azul afirmou que "está adotando medidas operacionais que podem resultar em ajustes na malha e nos horários de alguns voos".

A Latam, que encomendou modelos da Embraer, afirmou que não registrou anormalidade em seus voos porque só vai integrá-los à sua frota em dezembro. A Gol informou que não opera aeronaves dessa linha.

O g1 entrou em contato com a Embraer e aguarda posicionamento da empresa.

Passageiros que embarcariam em voos da Azul no Aeroporto Internacional de Brasília relataram cancelamentos e filas . Por volta das 20h30, ainda não havia informações se os voos seriam retomados na mesma noite ou remarcados.

A Infraero afirmou que seis voos da Azul foram cancelados no Aeroporto Santos Dumont, no Rio de Janeiro. Três deles tinham a cidade como destino, enquanto os outros três partiriam do aeroporto.

Leia abaixo a íntegra da nota divulgada pela Azul:

A Azul informa que uma instabilidade global no sistema de GPS está impactando a operação da frota Embraer E2. Por precaução, a Companhia está adotando medidas operacionais que podem resultar em ajustes na malha e nos horários de alguns voos.

A empresa orienta que os Clientes com voos impactados verifiquem o status de sua reserva nos canais oficiais da Companhia antes de se dirigir ao aeroporto.

Os Clientes estão recebendo a assistência prevista na Resolução 400 da Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac). A Azul ressalta que medidas operacionais são adotadas sempre com foco na segurança de suas operações, valor primordial para a Companhia.

articles.title: Ricardo Marques: candidato promete reduzir filas na saúde em Sergipe | G1
articles.standfirst: O candidato gravou programa eleitoral para rádio e televisão, participou de uma ação em seu comitê de campanha e reuniu-se com lideranças políticas.
articles.summary: Ricardo Marques detalha plano para saúde em Sergipe, prometendo reduzir filas e ampliar vagas na capital durante agenda de campanha nesta terça-feira.
articles.body:
Nesta terça-feira (22), o jornalismo do g1 e da TV Sergipe deu continuidade ao acompanhamento das agendas dos candidatos ao governo de Sergipe. A ordem de veiculação das matérias foi definida em reunião com representantes de todos os partidos e coligações.

O candidato Ricardo Marques (PL) gravou programa eleitoral para rádio e televisão, participou de uma ação em seu comitê de campanha e reuniu-se com lideranças políticas, em Aracaju . Ele falou à equipe da TV Sergipe sobre saúde.

Ricardo Marques, candidato ao governo de Sergipe — Foto: Reprodução/TV Sergipe

"Vamos falar sobre especialistas. Hoje em dia quem precisa de um especialista entra em uma fila e não sabe o dia do atendimento. Enquanto isso, a doença pode piorar e a família sofre. No meu governo, vamos reduzir filas levando especialistas para você no interior e ampliando vagas na capital. Ninguém vai precisar se humilhar para ter o que é de direito porque no meu governo a saúde das pessoas será prioridade", disse.

articles.standfirst: Candidata da Unidade Popular propõe ampliar o ensino integral para todas as escolas estaduais até 2030 e criar um auxílio-permanência para os alunos da rede.
articles.summary: Juliete Pantoja defende a universalização do ensino básico no Rio de Janeiro e a criação de um plano de carreira unificado para os professores da rede estadual.
articles.body:
A candidata ao governo do Rio de Janeiro pela Unidade Popular (UP), Juliete Pantoja, participou de uma manifestação estudantil nesta terça-feira (22), em Cabo Frio, na Região dos Lagos.

Durante o ato, a candidata falou sobre propostas para a educação e a valorização dos profissionais da área.

Juliete defendeu uma educação 100% gratuita e disse que, se eleita, pretende aumentar o número de vagas nas escolas e universidades para universalizar o acesso ao ensino básico e superior.

Ela propõe ampliar o ensino integral para todas as escolas estaduais até 2030 e criar um auxílio-permanência para os alunos da rede.

Juliete participou de manifestação estudantil em Cabo Frio, na Região dos Lagos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

A candidata também prevê a implantação de um plano de carreira unificado para os profissionais da educação básica, das escolas técnicas e das universidades estaduais, além da realização de concursos públicos para ampliar o número de servidores.

“Garantir todo o investimento na escola pública, garantir investimento na infraestrutura, na construção de novas escolas, na reabertura das escolas que já foram fechadas, garantir o piso nacional para os profissionais de educação, garantir concurso público. Educação pública 100% pública e gratuita.”

“Nessas estradas vicinais, tem que ser concreto, não dá mais. O asfalto não tem, porque cada localidade tem um tipo de solo. E esse tipo de solo, muitas vezes, o asfalto não se adapta e se perde com rapidez”, afirmou.

articles.title: Viagens por consulta, falta de remédio: os desafios da saúde em MG | G1
articles.standfirst: Especialistas e moradores apontam necessidade de descentralizar atendimento, garantir acesso a medicamentos e universalizar saneamento básico. Reportagem faz parte da série Minas Brasil, do MG2.
articles.summary: Especialistas apontam necessidade de descentralizar atendimento, garantir acesso a medicamentos e universalizar saneamento básico.
articles.body:
Viajar por mais de 12 horas, entre ida e volta, para uma única consulta médica. Ficar meses sem um remédio de alto custo que deveria ser fornecido pelo estado. Conviver com o esgoto correndo sob o quarto dos filhos e o risco de doenças. Essas são realidades que expõem as profundas desigualdades e os desafios na área da saúde em Minas Gerais.

Em um estado com dimensões continentais, o acesso a serviços de média e alta complexidade, a medicamentos e ao saneamento básico ainda não é universal, o que sobrecarrega a capital e deixa milhares de mineiros em situação de vulnerabilidade.

Em Belo Horizonte, a região hospitalar se tornou um "ponto de encontro" de ambulâncias de municípios de diversas regiões do estado, que transportam pacientes em busca de tratamento.

O aposentado Carlos Roberto da Mata mora em Ipanema, no Leste de Minas, e há 12 anos viaja para a capital mineira para tratar sequelas de um câncer. São 360 quilômetros de distância.

"É cansativo. Saio de lá meia-noite e chego aqui 6h30 da manhã", contou.

A vendedora Fátima Magalhães acompanha o marido. A cada viagem, a van da prefeitura só retorna a Ipanema após o atendimento médico de todos os ocupantes do veículo.

"A gente chega às vezes de madrugada em casa, porque outros pacientes precisam ser atendidos mais tarde. [...] É muito longe, tem que deixar tudo para acompanhar", disse.

Carlos Roberto da Mata e a esposa, Fátima Magalhães — Foto: TV Globo/ Reprodução

O estado é responsável por serviços de média e alta complexidade, como cirurgias, transplantes e tratamentos oncológicos. Também gerencia leitos de UTI, hemocentros, a rede de captação de órgãos e laboratórios de vigilância em saúde.

A Fundação Hospitalar do Estado de Minas Gerais (Fhemig) administra 14 hospitais, nove na Grande BH e cinco no interior.

Para Monique Félix, especialista em gestão de serviços de saúde da Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG, é preciso ampliar os hospitais regionais no interior, mas o mais importante é apoiar os municípios na rede de atenção à básica.

"O mesmo hospital é habilitado, por exemplo, em oncologia, em cardiologia, em neuro. E, no final das contas, ele não tem estrutura física, quantitativo de leitos necessário para atender todas as especialidades nas quais ele é habilitado. Isso sobrecarrega, inclusive, o sistema de transporte do próprio município", afirmou.

Além do atendimento, o estado é responsável por fornecer medicamentos, inclusive os de alto custo.

O aposentado Gilberto Marinho Vasconcelos caiu de uma ribanceira em 2010, e o acidente afetou as células responsáveis pela produção de hormônios. Um dos remédios que ele precisa para a reposição hormonal custa mais de R$ 800. Sem condições de pagar, ele conseguiu na Justiça o direito de receber o remédio, mas o fornecimento foi interrompido.

"A partir de abril, eu estive lá para pegar a próxima dosagem e fui surpreendido, quando o funcionário que me atendeu disse que estava em falta", contou.

Sem o medicamento, Gilberto sofre com cansaço, dores no corpo e indisposição.

"Eu não paguei porque estou sem dinheiro para fazer a compra desse remédio", disse.

Gilberto Marinho Vasconcelos — Foto: TV Globo/ Reprodução

A falta de saneamento básico é outro grave problema de saúde pública. Em Minas Gerais, 78,4% da população é atendida com rede coletora de esgoto. Embora tenha uma cobertura acima da média nacional (62,3%), a realidade em muitas comunidades é de risco e abandono.

Em Belo Horizonte, na casa de Kênia Yasmin, a fossa séptica fica embaixo do quarto dos filhos.

"A gente está até com medo. Meus meninos dormem aqui", contou.

Sem dinheiro para limpar a fossa entupida, a família construiu outra do lado de fora, a apenas um metro da tubulação de água, aumentando o risco de contaminação.

Os filhos de Kênia já tiveram vômitos e diarreias por causa da qualidade da água.

"Meu menino tem umas manchinhas no corpo que é da água também, o médico falou", disse.

Kênia Yasmin — Foto: TV Globo/ Reprodução

Na Ocupação Fábio Alves, na Região do Barreiro, 130 famílias também enfrentam a falta de saneamento.

"O pessoal adoece muito. O posto de saúde fica cheio, é tipo um vírus", afirmou a líder comunitária Simeia Rodrigues Rosa.

Segundo a especialista Monique Félix, a falta de saneamento impacta principalmente crianças e idosos.

"Isso se traduz em doenças infecciosas e parasitárias, sobrecarrega a urgência e emergência e tem impactos também para a questão da evasão escolar. Significa que a mulher, geralmente, nunca o pai, ter que se ausentar do trabalho para cuidar daquela criança. Então, tem um impacto para além da saúde, tem um impacto, inclusive, econômico e financeiro".

Em cidades como Congonhas, na Região Central, a preocupação é outra: a poluição gerada pela mineração. Moradora vizinha de uma mineradora, a empresária Ana Carolina Vieira convive com a poeira de minério.

"Se eu limpar a piscina hoje, amanhã ela já está toda suja de novo. Aqueles pretinhos lá são tudo minério. [...] Eu, meu filho, minha filha e meu marido, que trabalha na mineração... Está todo mundo passando mal esses dias", disse.

O estado é responsável pelo licenciamento ambiental da mineração e tem o dever de fiscalizar os impactos ambientais e à saúde da população.

"A literatura aponta diversos danos ao meio ambiente em relação à atividade mineradora. Isso causa de fato um aumento da poluição ambiental, muitas vezes também uma contaminação do solo, do lençol freático, e isso certamente também causa danos à saúde humana. [...] A atividade mineradora é uma atividade lícita, que agrega recursos para o estado, para a população, mas é papel do estado fiscalizar, regular, punir quando necessário, estabelecer limites e proteger os seus cidadãos", afirmou a pesquisadora e professora da Escola de Enfermagem da UFMG Deborah Malta.

articles.title: Video shows injured man on the ground after ICE mistakenly targets him
articles.summary: According to police, the man reported injuries to his head, neck, and teeth; DHS did not respond to questions about the man’s injuries or why ICE officers di...
articles.body:
A man is recovering from injuries he sustained Sunday morning after ICE officers mistakenly targeted him in a Chicago suburb.

In one video verified by NBC News, a Black man is seen sprawled on the street, near a curb, behind a black SUV in Evanston, Illinois. Two agents wearing ICE-style vests are seen standing over him. One of the agents has his face covered and is wearing a vest that reads "POLICE," and the other appears to be pinning the man down to the ground. The man is shouting at them and can be heard saying, "I'm a f------ U.S. citizen."

According to Evanston police , the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, and officers on the scene requested an ambulance.

Police said they are investigating the incident, which was recorded by bystanders and gained attention after being posted on social media.

One bystander in the background of the video is heard saying the ICE officers used force against the man. Other bystanders begin shouting at the man on the ground, asking him if he is OK. The ICE officers eventually get in the black SUV and drive off, leaving the man on the ground. The bystanders begin trying to help the man and call Evanston police.

"I saw two agents pinning down a gentleman. They were using very rough force on him, and it looked like they really did hurt him because we had to call 911," Miguel Angel Olivares, one of the people who witnessed the encounter, told NBC Chicago on Monday.

"When we saw him, he had his jaw swollen and he had a little blood on his shirt. I'm not sure if it was the agent's or it was his blood," Olivares said.

In a news release Sunday, Evanston police said they spoke to an ICE agent who said federal immigration officers "had attempted to identify an individual who resembled a person they were seeking." After the man refused to provide identification, he was "detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention."

An Evanston police officer reported observing blood on the agent's hands. The agent said he was injured while attempting to handcuff the individual and declined medical treatment, according to the news release from Evanston police. "Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a U.S. citizen. He was released."

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that their officers encountered a person who resembled someone they were targeting in an enforcement operation in Evanston on Sunday.

"ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself. ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself," the DHS statement reads. "DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence."

DHS did not state anything about the injuries the man suffered and why ICE officers did not appear to render aid.

Neither the police nor DHS identified the man who was injured.

Evanston police said they spoke with the injured man at a local hospital on Sunday. They "photographed and documented his injuries" as part of an ongoing investigation into the incident, police said.

articles.title: J&K scans 21 lakh library books, pulls out 4,000 titles; ‘objectionable content’ under scrutiny
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: J&K govt has pulled 4,249 books from public, school and college libraries, and sent another 1,752 titles for “expert examination” after .
articles.body: SRINAGAR: J&K govt has pulled 4,249 books from public, school and college libraries, and sent another 1,752 titles for “expert examination” after screening more than 21.8 lakh books for “objectionable content” over the past two months, education minister Sakina Itoo told the assembly Tuesday.The scrutiny follows orders issued in July by the education department and universities to screen all books — new and old — in offices, classrooms, staff rooms and libraries after the Union territory administration withdrew two books it called “highly inappropriate”. A year ago, the home department had banned 25 books on Kashmir for promoting “a false narrative”, “secessionism”, and “anti-national” views.Authorities have banned and removed 518 books so far. Of the 4,249 books withdrawn, 3,996 were from Kashmir and 253 from Jammu.The figures came in response to a question by MLA Khursheed Ahmad Sheikh of jailed MP Engineer Rashid’s Awami Ittihad Party, who accused govt of removing books related to Kashmir. “I have anything related to Kashmir issue or Kashmir is being removed from libraries of the universities and colleges. Even books by great writers on Kashmir are being removed… Do they want a bookless society in Kashmir?” he alleged.“We must be told what books are removed from circulation and why so,” Sheikh said, demanding that govt release their names. He also accused CM Omar Abdullah’s govt of facilitating what he called “large-scale targeting of Kashmir-related books and literature”.Itoo said in a written reply that “clear and objective criteria” were being used to identify objectionable material. Scrutiny of books was a “laborious exercise” and would take more time, she said, adding higher education institutions are expected to foster constitutional values, responsible citizenship and respect for India’s sovereignty, unity and integrity.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2025, an Australian couple launched an A$100,000 flat-pack pod on their Sunshine Coast farm; the tiny rental now earns about A$200,000 a year at near-full occupancy
articles.summary: Rest of World News: When mortgage repayments suddenly become the biggest expense on a dream property, adding another building might sound like an unlikely solution. For S.
articles.body: When mortgage repayments suddenly become the biggest expense on a dream property, adding another building might sound like an unlikely solution. For Sunshine Coast homeowners Sibel and Yalcin Karaman, however, a 6-metre-long glass pod on their farm has become a surprisingly powerful income generator. According to Real Estate website report, the couple invested about A$100,000 in the prefabricated tiny home after rising mortgage repayments put pressure on their finances. What took only three days to assemble has since developed into a sought-after short-term rental, bringing in about A$200,000 a year with occupancy running at roughly six nights out of seven.A tiny home with a big returnThe Elsewhere Pod sits on the couple's Sunshine Coast hinterland property and measures about 6 metres by 2.4 metres, states the online report. Its compact footprint is offset by floor-to-ceiling glass, contemporary interiors and a design aimed at making the most of its rural surroundings. Since launching in May 2025, bookings have doubled, with nightly rates ranging from A$220 to A$580 depending on demand, claims the report by Real Estate.The guest mix has also given the couple a steady stream of visitors. Around 60 per cent are Brisbane couples looking for a quick escape from the city, while domestic travellers make up roughly 30 per cent. International visitors account for as much as another 30 per cent, adds the online report. The pod operates alongside the couple's larger renovated farmhouse rental, creating two separate sources of accommodation income from the same property.Three days from flat pack to retreatThe speed of construction is one of the biggest attractions of the pod. Instead of a lengthy conventional building project, the structure arrived as a prefabricated flat-pack kit and was assembled on the property in just three days.That shorter construction timeline can reduce the disruption, labour requirements and uncertainty associated with traditional building projects, adds the online report data.For homeowners with suitable land, the concept offers another way to make underused space productive. A backyard pod can function as a holiday rental, guest accommodation, studio or longer-term living space without requiring the footprint of a conventional house.Part of Australia's tiny-home boomThe Karamans are part of a growing group of Australian property owners exploring modular accommodation as housing costs and mortgage pressures reshape the property market.Elsewhere Pods, the company behind the retreat, has expanded its range beyond compact studios. Its designs include granny flats and larger three-bedroom homes with wraparound verandahs, positioning modular construction as an option for investors, downsizers and families. The company now reports annual turnover of about A$9 million, with sales having doubled year-on-year since 2022.A changing idea of homeAustralia's tiny-home sector has expanded rapidly, with sales reportedly increasing by 120 per cent over five years. The Australian Tiny House Association estimates that more than 10,000 people now live in tiny homes or modular pods across the country, adds the report. And for the Karamans, the appeal is less about downsizing than making their existing property work harder. Their glass pod has transformed a relatively small patch of their farm into a high-demand getaway, while providing an additional income stream alongside the main rental.Image Courtesy: Real EstateCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Fishing charter reels in suspected US military drone off Florida coast, believed to be Iranian-designed Shahed-136 clone; Eglin Air Force Base confirms test article went down
articles.summary: US News: A routine fishing trip off Florida’s Panhandle took an unexpected turn when a group aboard a fishing charter reportedly hauled in a US military drone .
articles.body: A routine fishing trip off Florida’s Panhandle took an unexpected turn when a group aboard a fishing charter reportedly hauled in a US military drone believed to be a clone of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136.Hot Spots Charters, a fishing company based in Pensacola, shared photographs of the unusual catch on Facebook, showing the drone lying aboard the vessel alongside more conventional fishing catches.“Great 6 hour today with this crew! If anyone is looking for their drone please call Hot Spots!” charter captain Daniel Arsenault wrote in the post.Drone reportedly recovered near Eglin Air Force BaseThe discovery was reportedly made in waters near Eglin Air Force Base, which is home to the US Air Force’s 96th Test Wing.According to defense publication The War Zone, an Eglin Air Force Base spokesperson confirmed that a drone had gone missing from the base’s inventory, although the Air Force did not identify the model.“I can confirm that we were doing a test and the test article went down,” the spokesperson told The War Zone.Arsenault told CNN that he encountered the aircraft by chance while offshore.“Riding along offshore and saw it floating,” he said.Drone appears to be US-made Shahed-136 cloneThe aircraft photographed aboard the fishing boat appeared to be an FLM 136, a US-produced replica of Iran’s Shahed-136, a one-way attack drone that has featured prominently in conflicts involving Ukraine and Iran.The US Air Force announced late last year that it had developed a clone of the Iranian-designed aircraft under the Low-cost Unmanned Combat Attack System, or LUCAS, programme.The drones are manufactured by Arizona-based SpektreWorks. According to the information provided in the report, the aircraft are approximately 9.8 feet (2.9 metres) long, have a wingspan of 8.2 feet and weigh about 70 pounds.US Central Command announced in early March that LUCAS drones were being used in the war with Iran, describing their deployment as “delivering American-made retribution.”Drone recovered with missing nose and propellerPhotographs shared by Hot Spots Charters showed the aircraft with its nose section missing and damage to the rear, including the propeller.The fishing company later posted an update indicating that the drone had been collected.“The black suvs came and got their drone, all is good!” the company wrote on Facebook.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Swedish woman digging for fishing bait near Stockholm uncovered 24,100 silver coins, making it the country’s largest medieval coin hoard
articles.summary: Europe News: A woman digging for fishing bait near her summer house in the Stockholm area uncovered what has since been identified as Sweden's largest coin hoard. .
articles.body: A woman digging for fishing bait near her summer house in the Stockholm area uncovered what has since been identified as Sweden's largest coin hoard. The discovery was made in 2025 on the Mörkö peninsula near Södertälje and contained approximately 24,100 silver coins alongside 144 other objects. The hoard dates from the Viking Age and early Middle Ages, with most of the coins dating to the 12th century. Its total weight is now reported at about 4.7 kilograms. After the discovery was reported to the Stockholm County Administrative Board, archaeologists examined the material and the surrounding site before the find was assessed by Sweden's National Heritage Board, the Riksantikvarieämbetet. In May 2026, the authority decided to redeem the hoard for 4 million Swedish kronor, recognising its exceptional archaeological and historical value.Thousands of silver coins were found near a summer houseThe discovery happened while the woman was digging for fishing bait near her summer house. She and her husband reported the find to the authorities, allowing archaeologists to investigate the discovery and document the objects. The initial announcement by the Stockholm County Administrative Board described the discovery as an unusually large silver hoard from the early Middle Ages. At that stage, the number of coins had not yet been established, with an initial estimate suggesting that there could be around 20,000.Further examination subsequently established that the hoard contained approximately 24,100 silver coins and 144 additional objects. The collection weighs about 4.7 kilograms according to later Swedish reporting. The exact location of the discovery has been kept confidential while the archaeological work has been carried out. The material was subsequently assessed by the National Heritage Board, which considered its archaeological and historical significance when determining whether the state should redeem it.Most of the coins date to the 12th centuryThe majority of the coins date from the 12th century. Some bear the inscription “KANUTUS”, the Latin form of the name Knut, and are associated with King Knut Eriksson, who ruled Sweden during the latter part of the 12th century. The hoard also contains unusual examples of medieval coinage known as bishop coins. Rather than being associated with a reigning king, these coins were issued in connection with bishops. Several examples depict a figure holding a crozier, the hooked staff traditionally associated with a bishop.Other coins are connected to Gotland. Some feature imagery that may represent a church building, although the interpretation is presented by the authorities as a possibility rather than a certainty. The mixture of royal, ecclesiastical and Gotlandic coinage makes the collection particularly significant to researchers studying the monetary and social history of medieval Sweden.The final examination made it Sweden's largest coin hoardWhen the discovery was first announced in September 2025, archaeologists did not yet know the final number of coins. The Stockholm County Administrative Board said at the time that the hoard could contain around 20,000. The subsequent examination produced a larger total of approximately 24,100 silver coins, together with 144 other objects. The National Heritage Board now identifies the discovery, known as the Hörningsholm hoard, as the largest coin hoard ever found in Sweden.The authority has also highlighted the unusually large number of bishop coins among the finds. Beyond the coins, the 144 additional objects contribute further archaeological information about the collection and the period in which it was buried. The National Heritage Board said the hoard has significant cultural and historical value because discoveries of this scale can provide information about Sweden's economy, contacts and society during the Viking Age and early Middle Ages.The finder will receive 4 million kronor from the stateSwedish heritage legislation requires certain archaeological finds containing precious metals to be reported to the authorities and made available for possible redemption by the state. The finder reported the discovery to the Stockholm County Administrative Board, allowing the authorities to take custody of the archaeological material and assess it. In May 2026, the National Heritage Board decided to redeem the Hörningsholm hoard for 4 million Swedish kronor. The authority said its assessment of the compensation took into account the exceptional cultural and historical value of the discovery as well as the need for redemption payments to remain reasonable. The decision means that the hoard will become part of Sweden's archaeological heritage rather than remaining in private possession. Its approximately 24,100 silver coins and 144 additional objects provide researchers with an unusually substantial collection from the Viking Age and early Middle Ages, all originating from a single buried find near Stockholm.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kratom found at locations where two Ole Miss students were discovered dead
articles.summary: Two University of Mississippi students died this week and packaged kratom was found during the separate death investigations, law enforcement officials said Tuesday.
articles.body: Two University of Mississippi students died this week and packaged kratom was found during the separate death investigations, law enforcement officials said Tuesday. Authorities said they have not confirmed that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death. Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said Tuesday that it has no information that the two deaths are linked. “However, packaged Kratom sold from a retail store was found during both investigations,” it said in a statement. “Out of an abundance of caution, we encourage everyone to avoid kratom and any other medication or substance that was not prescribed to you or obtained from a trusted, regulated source.” The Ole Miss students have not been publicly identified by authorities. Both were found dead Monday; one on campus, and the other in the city of Oxford, Mayor Robyn Tannehill said. “The University is heartbroken by the recent loss of two students and extends our condolences to their families, friends, and loved ones during this difficult time,” the university said. The deaths, which are under investigation by local, state and federal authorities, are being treated as separate inquiries, according to Lafayette County Metro Narcotics. Raegan Settle, a senior who is the student editor-in-chief of the student newspaper “The Daily Mississippian,” said the mood on campus was “really frantic.” A lot of the details were just coming out Tuesday, she said. “Many students are hanging black ribbons around their sorority and fraternity houses as we speak,” she said. “So, I think people are just really shocked.” Greek organizations on campus have been reminding members not to take anything that is not prescribed specifically for them by their doctor, Settle said. Kratom, the name of a product and the Southeast Asia tree from which it comes, has gained popularity in the U.S. as an unapproved treatment for pain, anxiety and drug dependence. It is sometimes sold at gas stations or online. Kratom can produce either stimulating or sedating effects, depending on the dosage taken, and can produce psychotic symptoms, according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. It’s not federally banned, but the DEA lists it as a “drug and chemical of concern.” The Mayo Clinic calls kratom unsafe and ineffective and says it’s been linked to a small number of deaths, but that “nearly all deaths from kratom also involved other drugs or substances.” Kratom has been banned by local laws in Oxford, Mississippi, but can be bought in surrounding counties, said Capt. Alex Fauver, commander of the Metro Narcotics unit. “We have a lot of problems with the kratom and people on it, it has no medical use,” he said in a phone interview. Kratom was found at each student’s residence, he said. There have been no other student deaths and no other students or members of the community impacted, Fauver and the university said. Authorities urged people not to speculate, and acknowledged that there was unverified information being spread online. Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said there was a “significant amount of concern, speculation, and misinformation circulating.”

articles.title: New York City Bakery Selling $60 Loaf of Bread Goes Viral, Owner Explains Reason Behind the Cost
articles.summary: A bit of dough is going to cost you some major dough at one New York City bakery. Rye, a bakery in NYC owned by Austrian baker Martin Auer, went viral after...
articles.body:
Rye bakery in NYC is selling a $60 sourdough loaf that weighs 3.3 pounds, attributing the high price to the efforts and costs involved in making it.

The bakery imports organic rye flour from Austria and follows a meticulous process of fermenting the sourdough, shaping the bread, and allowing it to rest for 12 hours after baking.

In addition to bread, Rye bakery offers spreads, toppings, and accessories like branded ballcaps, canvas totes, tumblers, cutting boards, and leather loafers ranging from $80 to $160.

A bit of dough is going to cost you some major dough at one New York City bakery.

Rye , a bakery in NYC owned by Austrian baker Martin Auer , went viral after social media caught wind of their $60 sourdough — but the mastermind behind the loaf claims the price is justified.

"First of all, it's a lot of bread," co-owner Tim Auer told People on Tuesday, September 22. "It's about 3.3 pounds, and we not only sell the whole loaf for $60, but we also sell half a loaf or a quarter of the loaf for either $30 or $15."

He explained that the high price tag is a "result of all the efforts and costs" that go into each loaf, which is made with just water, flour and salt, per the New York Post , noting that New Yorkers are lining up to buy it.

"Whether that's importing the organic rye flour from Austria or baking it right here on site on Lafayette Street," Tim added. "You need to ferment the rye sourdough. You need to feed it every day. That takes about 24 hours before you can use it again. Then you need to make the dough, ferment the dough of the bread, shave the bread, ferment the dough again, bake it, and then you have to let it rest."

According to Tim — whose bakery is located near the border of SoHo and NoLiTa in Manhattan — explained that even after baking, each loaf needs to rest for 12 hours before it can be cut or sold.

"It's all about the craft and our appreciation for craftsmanship, and for doing something that is inherently simple exceptionally well," he told the outlet. "That's why we built the space the way we did with this open bakery where you can actually watch the baker do this, and bake rye and shape the bread every day."

In addition to loaves, the family sells spreads and toppings, as well as accessories ranging from an $80 branded ballcap, $90 canvas tote, various tumblers, cutting boards, and a $160 pair of leather loafers.

articles.title: Ahead of ‘firing’ deaths anniversary, promise of Article 371 framework for Ladakh
articles.summary: India News: Srinagar: Two days ahead of the first anniversary of four deaths in alleged police firing on protesters in Leh demanding Sixth Schedule status and sta.
articles.body: Srinagar: Two days ahead of the first anniversary of four deaths in alleged police firing on protesters in Leh demanding Sixth Schedule status and statehood on Sept 24 last year, Ladakh authorities promised Tuesday a new framework under Article 371 to provide constitutional safeguards suited to the Union territory’s (UT) specific requirements.In an interaction with prominent community members in Leh, chief secretary Ashish Kundra signalled broad agreement on the need for such safeguards. “The protection should cover our land, employment, culture, environment and natural resources,” he said.According to Kundra, the new framework being worked out “considering the aspirations of Ladakhis does not exist anywhere else in the country”. The draft will be discussed at the next meeting with Ladakh groups in the first week of Oct. The last such meeting with the Centre was held in Delhi on Sept 9.Kundra listed direct elections to a proposed UT-level body as a key suggestion emerging from the discussions. “Further steps, including consideration of the proposed constitutional amendment by Parliament, would follow after consensus is reached on the framework,” he said.Kundra explained that a separate legislation would be required for powers, functions and institutional arrangements of the proposed body.Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), two main organisations negotiating with the Union home ministry (MHA) on the region’s autonomy, have been in such talks since 2023.The process stopped after four people were killed and over 80 injured in the firing last year. LAB member and activist Sonam Wangchuk was accused of inciting the protesters, arrested, charged under NSA and kept in Jodhpur jail. The Centre revoked his NSA detention in March this year. After his release, Wangchuk has pressed for talks. He attended the Sept 9 meeting.At Tuesday’s interaction, chief secretary Kundra highlighted also recent initiatives like strengthening district-level administrative structures and progress towards panchayat elections. He flagged a surge in tourist arrivals, saying four lakh visitors came to Ladakh this year, up from 3.35 lakh in all of 2025.Ladakh DGP Anand Jain made a presentation on drug-related issues and sought civil society’s support in spreading awareness.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The best editor-approved planners to make even the most hectic schedules more manageable
articles.summary: I rounded up some of the best planners and agendas to help you get organized this year, complete with calendars, to-do lists and more.
articles.body: Things like smart clocks, digital calendars and to-do lists help you stay organized and on top of your routine. Traditional planners also keep your schedule on track and typically don’t come at a high price either. Finding the best planner for your personal routine, however, involves more than simply picking up the first one you see. Depending on your routine, the best planner or agenda for you will likely have more than just blank paper — it should come with features like calendars, tabs, sections for to-do lists, lists of important dates and holidays, and at the least, lined pages. Plus, a great planner should be able to keep up with your lifestyle, which means it has to have a durable cover to help keep it together for months. To find the best planners and agendas for this year, I gathered recommendations from my colleagues and included options from brands I’ve used myself. Read more about our favorite analog planners below. This hardcover planner is available as a mid-year planner and as an academic year option. It’s available in several styles and it includes calendars and weekly planning sections for each month. It also has a section for dates, reminders, contact information and more. Each calendar also has a section on the side for important notes. In addition to the weekly planning sections and calendars and daily to-do lists, the back of the planner also has dotted and lined pages for additional note taking. It also has a ribbon to place between pages to help keep your place. The planner, which has 192 pages, is available as a hardcover or as a softer spiral-bound option. This planner is a favorite of NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans, who says she loves it because it allows her to physically check boxes off of her to-do list. “I particularly like this planner because it gives me enough room for my extensive lists (unlike some previous puny planners I’ve owned) and it does 30-minute time slots for my appointments,” she says. “One of my favorite features is the space to add my meals and water intake, and yes, I fill this in daily — my nutritionist would be so proud.” Since it’s a full-size planner (read: large), it is better for keeping in one place, like your office desk, rather than trekking back and forth daily, according to Evans. Also, while it isn’t dated, it’s a daily planner, so it’s best if used for day-of obligations as opposed to for planning weeks or months in advance. Available in 20 colors, this planner from Amazon comes with a ribbon bookmark, an elastic band and 160 lined pages. It is also available in blank, dotted and 252-page options and you can also get it in multipacks. While it doesn’t have calendars and pre-made to-do lists, it’s far from plain, but great for people who want a simple planner that also doesn’t cost a ton of money. It has a pocket on the inside and it comes with multiple lined adhesive labels, which you can use to write your name, contact information and other important details in case you lose it. It’s also compact enough to fit in a small tote or purse, which is useful if you want to travel to and from work or school with it. “I’m not picky about journals. I really just need a notebook that isn’t too big or small and has a decent amount of pages,” says Nikki Brown, NBC Selected senior editor. “I love the basic-ness and dependability of Paperage notebooks. I always keep one in my bag and find the cover to be durable despite everything it rubs up against in my work bag.” Unlike the other Papier planners above, this one is undated, so while it has calendars and pages for days of the week, they aren’t filled in. You can add the month or day of the week yourself and you can customize the calendar with your own important events in addition to holidays. It has 365 pages — so you could plan out the entire year — and there are pages with grids in the back, for mathematical work. Plus, you can have your name and the year added to the front of the planner if you really want to add some custom details. NBC Selected editorial operations associate Jem Alabi has this planner and says it helps keep her organized. “Other than the fact that it’s undated (which saves me the shame of forgetting a day or two when I’m traveling or really busy), the page layout is priority-based which reflects the way my brain works,” she says. “As someone who has to-do lists for my work, home, and social life, I can keep all my tasks in this one planner.” Best daily planner This softcover option from Papier is perfect if you prefer something with a more flexible feel and spiral binding that you can use to hold your writing tool. It has a calendar for every month in 2027, each of which has holidays and themed months listed as well as a sidebar for writing notes and reminders. It also has a section for monthly goals, lined sections to use for to-do lists, weekly grids and blank areas for sketching and more. The top of each lined section also has bullets for writing important tasks for each month. The planner can be purchased in a hard cover option too. Best large-size planner I first bought this planner because I prefer the large size over the small planners, so it’s great for people who enjoy something that is closer to the size of regular copy paper. It has tabs for each month, starting from the middle of 2026 and all the way to the end of 2027. It has monthly calendars as well as mini calendars on the edges of the pages (sometimes called reference calendars), weekly sections with lined areas for each day, pages for writing contact information, a map of the United States and a list of major holidays. I like using it at my desk for when I’m home and planning personal errands. Also, being left handed, the size of the planner makes it easier to write in it compared to smaller options. I also love the side tabs for each month because they let me find any month in a few seconds. Best faux leather planner NBC Selected editor Mili Godio put a lot of thought into buying the right planner and spent a lot of time shopping before landing on this one from Sterling Ink. “The Common Planner kept popping up over and over, and when I finally pulled the plug on the $60 planner, I understood why it’s so popular,” she says. “It’s extremely basic, which is exactly what I wanted; it has a month-to-month calendar, weekly pages, quarterly pages and yearly/monthly trackers — no quotes, designs, holidays or moon phases that I find take up unnecessary space.” Her favorite feature of the planner is that it has blank pages in the back that she uses a lot to jot down to-dos and deadlines.” How I picked the best planners Here is everything I factored into the list of planners above. Most of the options I included are based on products our staff has used before. Dates and calendars: The most important part of any planner is how it organizes all of the dates throughout the year, including months, days of the week and holidays. Some planners have a mix of calendars with sections on the sides for notes and sections with every few pages representing the days of the week. Some planners have slightly more plain designs, with blank calendars and lined sections for notes without dates. I made sure to include different styles of planners, mostly with at least one organizational feature (calendars, dates, etc.). I only included one option that has just lined pages (Paperage Lined Journal Notebook), for those who prefer a very basic planner. Material and style: I also considered the material and style of different planners available, mainly whether or not they had hard or soft covers. Hardcover planners are generally more durable than softcover planners, so they can handle being moved around a lot, put into backpacks and more, but they aren’t always as lightweight as some spiral-bound softcover planners. Softcover planners typically aren’t as bulky to carry as hardcover options, but they tend to get damaged quickly comparatively. With this in mind, I included both styles as well as options with internal pockets and more. Customization: In making the list of planners above, I made sure to include options that, in addition to having the basic features of a planner, also offer fun features or customizations, like sticker labels, built-in bookmarks for easily finding your page, reminders to stay hydrated, maps, sections for contact information and more. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a commerce editor at NBC Selected, where I write about lifestyle, organization, home storage and more. I’ve written about closet organizing products, dorm room essentials for college students, label-making devices and more. For this story I received recommendations from different NBC Selected staffers (and used my own favorites) who are pretty busy and regularly use planners to keep their schedules organized. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence 'creating, not cutting' jobs in Newport
articles.summary: One school even offers pupils a semiconductor qualification to help them get into the industry.
articles.body:
"I think there's a huge fear of AI taking away jobs. It's quite the opposite here," said Jutta Meier, who leads one of Wales' most successful semiconductor companies.

In a vast metal building on the edge of the M4, scientists and engineers at IQE wear futuristic overalls as they create the chips that fuel the revolution in artificial intelligence (AI).

"We are growing great jobs based on AI and supporting AI, quite the opposite from destroying jobs by AI," Meier said.

The UK's AI minister Kanishka Narayan said Wales had to "reindustrialise itself" for an AI future, while also "supporting everyone who is affected" by changing technology.

Newport has established a cluster of semiconductor companies, with IQE in production since 1988 and the wider cluster is growing.

An independent report for CSconnected, produced by Cardiff University's Welsh Economy Research Unit, found the south Wales compound semiconductor sector supported 3,140 jobs across Wales in 2025, up from 2,748 a year earlier , a 14% increase.

Of those, 1,914 were direct jobs in the industry, concentrated around Newport and the wider M4 corridor.

The report said average salaries in the sector were about £66,000.

Office for National Statistics data estimated the median monthly pay in the UK in August was £2,657 - or £31,884 a year .

Nearby Bassaleg School in Newport now offers a semiconductor qualification to students who are keen to join the industry.

IQE has benefited from the recent boom in AI because its chips are part of the physical architecture of data centres.

They are not connected to the algorithms that allow humans to interact with chatbots, but are found in the computer hardware that underpins the operation.

"The last 18 months were quite bumpy," Meier admits, as IQE struggled for relevance with investors.

Earlier this year its role in data centre computing power was acknowledged and its share price grew quickly, allowing the firm to clear debts and begin hiring more staff.

The impact of AI on jobs has been evident recently with tech giant Oracle slashing 21,000 roles globally as it reshaped its business around the technology.

Amazon and Facebook-owner Meta have also cut thousands of jobs in recent months as they invest heavily in AI.

But Meier said: "We're really lucky to have a very dedicated workforce that stuck with us throughout this bumpy road.

"Talent, for IQE, is one of the biggest assets that we have."

Two miles from IQE, students at Bassaleg School are among the first in the UK to be offered a semiconductor qualification.

Head teacher Victoria Lamb said it allowed students to learn about an industry that was "right on their doorstep".

She said it was "important that we work with our community to offer pupils these kinds of opportunities".

"It is really good fun," said 15-year-old Grace.

"We are doing practical work, and before the course I used to think semiconductors were all on a computer."

Grace said it was "pretty cool" to have the semiconductor industry in the city.

Her classmate Evan, who counts soldering as a hobby, welcomed the chance to put the skills into practice in school.

"I think semiconductors will play a big role in what I want to do," he said.

"I want to go into the electro-mechanical side, making robots. And semiconductors play a massive role in making that possible."

Evan said there were "so many different companies, especially around Newport" offering careers after leaving school.

Kanishka Narayan, the UK government's AI minister, said Wales' "amazing heritage in manufacturing" needed to be applied to the growth in AI.

"The biggest economic opportunity for us is how we create more manufacturing jobs here in Wales, re-industrialise ourselves, hark back to our heritage but for a more durable future and AI is going to be a big part of it," he told BBC Wales.

The semiconductor cluster was "paying 40 to 50% higher wages" than many other sectors in the area, Narayan said.

But he warned that the boom in AI-related jobs would come at a cost.

"I think in all industrial change of the past, there have been some jobs created, some jobs lost.

"The task for us as a society is to make sure that we're supporting everyone who is affected and creating opportunities for our kids, for their kids as well."

While the chips are powering the AI revolution, there are already examples in Wales where the technology is creating new roles and changing existing jobs.

At TiqToq, a Welsh software engineering firm that helps companies to search for security flaws in its systems, the company said AI was initially viewed as a cost-saving opportunity.

"But that's not been the story at all," said director Mike Beck.

AI meant the work of its human engineers was now "much more efficient" and their use of AI to help stress-test their clients' software had led to "over 53% time saving" for employees.

The pace allowed the company to hire more people, while AI became a key tool in completing tasks for clients.

"What we've found is that the projects that our customers were looking to release next year, they'll now bring them forward to this year," Beck said, adding that engineers were now "focusing on the areas that require that extra human insight".

In other cases, AI is reducing the burden of paperwork facing frontline health and support staff.

Social workers in Vale of Glamorgan are testing Beam Notes transcription software that records and summarises their interactions with clients, cutting the time it takes to produce the paperwork associated with their roles.

"You know it's going to capture all the information you need, without worrying about writing everything down," said social worker Sian Palmer.

The technology was "absolutely not" replacing people, Palmer said, and it was enhancing interactions with clients.

"It's obviously a time saver, and for me I've got dyslexia, so for me it's always been a bit of an added stress, I suppose, in making sure my assessments are up to the level they need to be."

Using the AI transcription tool was "just a way of sort of gathering the information in great detail, in a fast way," she said.

articles.title: Council leaders wary of radical plan to redraw Scotland's local government map
articles.summary: Local politicians across Scotland are digesting plans for the biggest shake-up of the council system in 30 years.
articles.body:
Council leaders have been voicing their concerns about proposals for the biggest shake up of local government in 30 years.

Some have warned Scottish government plans to potentially streamline the number of authorities from 32 to six will not save money.

Others have questioned the potential impact on rural parts and the "absurd" timeline.

Under proposals for a new two-tier system , the regional bodies would focus on major issues such as education and economic growth.

Between 120 and 160 community authorities would also be created, contributing to local issues such as licensing and town centre improvements.

Scotland's 32 councils could be cut to six under government plan

The changes, which would fundamentally reshape a system that has existed since 1996, have now been shared with Holyrood's committees and council umbrella body Cosla ahead of a public consultation.

The Scottish government argues that some of these councils are too large to be truly local but too small to be strategic.

For almost 20 years there has been talk of councils working together more closely to share overheads and cut duplication - for instance sharing responsibility for road maintenance or back office functions.

But less has happened than had originally been expected and the talk now is of a fundamental overhaul.

Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth has described the proposals as a "starting point" for reform.

She said: "We need to ensure investment is focused on frontline delivery, with the right staff in the right roles to empower communities and deliver real improvements in public services."

"Existing local government responsibilities could also be extended, including enhanced roles in economic development and business support so that individual areas can reflect local strengths and ambitions."

The broad signals from the Scottish government at present seem to draw some inspiration from aspects of the two previous systems of local government in Scotland:

Large regional councils - which existed from 1975 to 1996 - which had responsibility for major services like education.

The old town councils - abolished in 1975 - which provided local services for distinct communities, sometimes of only a few thousand people.

They worked together with county councils.

There are no indications at present of the likely geographical boundaries of the new authorities.

Nor is there any indication of just how they would be funded.

Would the community bodies have tax raising powers of their own?

Or would the existing funding system be amended?

Inevitably this discussion may become intertwined with the question of replacing the council tax. So what do the current council leaders make of it?

Perth and Kinross Council will be one of the first to fully debate the proposals on Wednesday.

Council leader Eric Drysdale, told BBC Scotland News he wanted them to be "a starting point for discussion rather than any final decision".

"That's why I believe it is vital to ensure that Perth and Kinross has a strong voice in the national conversation which is taking place about public service reform."

Drysdale said the local authority already fulfilled many of the ambitions associated with public service reform through its partnership working, housing investment, employability support and collaboration with neighbouring authorities.

He added: "We have valuable experience to contribute that other parts of Scotland could benefit from."

But David Ross, leader of Fife Council, has questioned the very need for such fundamental structural reform - and does not think it will save money.

He said it would be "much simpler and more effective" to maintain the status quo but allow local authorities to "merge if they wished" and to collaborate through city region and local growth deals.

Ross proposed that they should also be trusted to develop local arrangements for "community empowerment".

The council leader added: "Most local government services cannot simply be broken down into 'community areas' or they lose the economies of scale and operational efficiencies.

"Anyone who went through the last local government reorganisation in 1995/96 knows the complexity and disruption of this process and if the first minister thinks there will be any financial savings from the process then he is sadly mistaken."

Once actual proposals for the boundaries of the new regions and community bodies emerge, they may well prove controversial too.

One senior figure within Scottish local government that he thought the idea of six regions was simply a starting point or negotiating position.

He thought around 10 would be more realistic.

Fundamental change costs money to begin with - any savings are achieved over the longer term.

Another council leader, Brian Connolly, who heads up South Ayrshire Council, wants the costs of reorganisation to be met by the Scottish government.

He said: "The merits or otherwise of a regional approach can be debated but it is essential that local views and decision-making are maintained, along with substantial transfer of powers."

Connolly added the three Ayrshire councils already have a "strong history of working together".

Given their proximity and links it is possible that Edinburgh, the three Lothian councils and the Scottish Borders could be within the same region.

But Euan Jardine, leader of Scottish Borders Council, said: "My biggest concern is rural Scotland.

"The Borders is a huge rural area made up of towns, villages and communities spread over a massive geography."

He highlighted issues such as transport, access to services matters and local identity.

Jardine said: "The Scottish government has rightly recognised that island communities may need bespoke arrangements because geography matters.

"Well, rural mainland Scotland deserves the same thinking.

"You cannot take a model that might work in one part of Scotland and assume it will work everywhere else."

The council leader said there were still "huge unanswered questions" in relation to local authority workers.

He added: "Who employs people? Where are they based? Who are they accountable to? What happens to existing council teams and local jobs? None of that is clear yet."

The leader of City of Edinburgh Council, Jane Meagher, also has questions and is worried the plan could be rushed through.

She said it was unclear how community authorities would work and how they would be funded.

Meagher told BBC Scotland News: "What this might mean for Edinburgh Council remains to be seen.

"The timescale for such consequential and far-reaching reforms doesn't lend itself to serious and considered discussion with the Scottish government."

"Eleven weeks to decide the future of public services in the country is absurd."

East Lothian Council leader Norman Hampshire said his administration supported the current structure of 32 local authorities bolstered by regional partnerships in priorities such as economic development and transport.

On the other side of Scotland, Argyll and Bute is a geographically vast, rural council - stretching from the Glasgow commuter zone to tiny islands like Tiree and Iona.

It was already looking at options for reform.

The so-called Single Authority Model would see the council and other local public services, such as the NHS, come together formally and work much more closely than at present. It is still keen on this approach.

Jim Lynch, is the leader of Argyll and Bute Council, which has the highest number of inhabited islands in Scotland.

He welcomed the Sottish government's indication that it wanted to "identify a shared direction for public service reform".

But Lynch added: "There is also the question of whether larger local government regions would still be able to reflect local needs and identities.

One of the most surprising results of local government reoganisation in the 1990s was the creation of Clackannanshire Council.

The smallest mainland council centred around Alloa serves around 52,000 people.

Council leader Ellen Forson says the council cannot ignore challenges and is always keen to work with neighbouring councils and other public bodies.

But she believes the council area itself works.

She said: "We are large enough to deliver effectively, but small enough to understand our communities, respond quickly and maintain a close connection between local people and those making decisions on their behalf."

The reaction so far gives a foretaste of the intensity of the debate which is likely once solid proposals are published.

Blair McDougall, Labour MP for East Renfrewshire, has warned of the risk of the area - which includes some of Glasgow's affluent suburbs - being absorbed into what he fears could be a larger city authority.

In the 1990s Labour fought to save Strathclyde Region and opposed the redrawing of Glasgow's boundaries.

The reorganisation was opposed by most Scottish MPs and many within Scottish local government.

That level of controversy is unlikely this time.

The proposals will come from Holyrood and the SNP has more councillors than any other party.

But the powers of the new authorities, the practicalities of change and the simple geography of some council areas are still likely to provoke a huge discussion.

articles.title: US Republican calls for probe into Donald Trump Jr’s business dealings
articles.summary: US Senator John Curtis’s letter marks a rare effort by a member of the president’s own party to hold him accountable.
articles.body:
A member of Donald Trump’s political party has issued a rare call for a congressional investigation into the foreign dealings of the United States president’s eldest son.

US Senator John Curtis, a Republican from the state of Utah, on Tuesday said “questions have arisen” about Donald Trump Jr’s relationships with foreign business figures and acceptance of “significant gifts”, alleging he may have personally benefited from his relationship with the president.

In a letter to the Republican and Democratic leaders of the US Senate Judiciary Committee, Curtis referenced a ProPublica report that found Trump Jr’s Bahamian wedding party in May was funded by a Russian oligarch.

“These reports raise legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president’s family and whether such relationships can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment,” Curtis wrote. “They also may create expectations of a returned favor that would not be in the best interests of the American people or our allies, and could even create national security vulnerabilities.”

The letter comes as a small but slowly growing number of Republicans have spoken out against Trump, who has largely avoided criticism from members of his own party. But record-low approval ratings sparked by the war in Iran and concerns over the cost of living in the US have forced some Republicans to reconsider that support as they face growing prospects of major losses in the congressional midterm elections.

If Democrats retake one, or both, chambers of the US Congress in November, investigations into Trump, including his family’s dealings, are likely. But those probes are less likely under Republicans wary of the president’s wrath.

A spokesperson for the Senate Judiciary Committee, which is under Republican control, told the Associated Press that it had received Curtis’s letter but did not say whether there would be an investigation.

Curtis, who isn’t up for re-election until 2030, also called on the chamber’s panel to subpoena Trump Jr, as well as the son of former US President Joe Biden, a Democrat.

“The country should not have to accept one standard for the family of a Republican president and another for the family of a Democratic president,” Curtis wrote, referencing the scrutiny and investigation Biden’s son Hunter faced from Republicans.

Hunter Biden responded to Curtis’s letter in a post on social media, calling for the Senate committee to “bring it on” as he vehemently denied any foreign business dealings while his father was president.

“I’ll sit next to Don Jr. and testify any time, any place,” Biden wrote on X as he called for the president’s youngest son, Eric, and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who serves as a US envoy, to testify as well. “No need for a subpoena. Let’s all do it tomorrow.”

After the ProPublica report, Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, released a joint statement on social media saying the Russian oligarch, Umar Kremlev, was a “dear friend” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding”.

The president, who did not attend the wedding, said his son had reimbursed Kremlev.

“It’s totally allowed, and a lot of people give parties and things like that — but it’s totally allowed,” Trump said. “But as I understand it, he paid him back. He didn’t want it.”

US Senator Dick Durbin, the ranking member on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said that while Biden’s son “has already given a sworn deposition to Congress”, Trump Jr “has not”.

“For the committee to ignore this matter is to run the risk of being complicit in a coverup,” Durbin said. “I will join in supporting Senator Curtis’ request of the Senate Judiciary Committee.”

Curtis’s office did not immediately reply when asked by Al Jazeera what prompted the senator’s letter and whether any fellow Republicans have indicated if they would support an investigation into the president’s family.
